title: The Long River
part: PART ONE: TWO WAYS OF KNOWING

pages.text:
*Jun's phone says: 33 degrees, sunny, 85%. Nari's river says: brown-green, easy, low.*

The path through the corn was green and tight, and Jun’s white sneakers remained spotless, a fact he held onto like a small, bright shield. Nari did not look at them. She walked ahead, her braid swinging, her straw hat bouncing on her back.

"Keep up," she said, without turning.

They emerged from the leaves onto a wide bank of pale sand, where the Long River lay ahead, brown-green and slow. It did not rush. It slid, smooth and heavy, carrying the light of the sun in a long, shining sheet. Sandbars rose from the water like the backs of sleeping animals, their edges soft and rounded.

Jun’s phone showed a map. The map said he was at the river. The river said nothing.

Nari stopped at the edge. She looked down at the water, squinting, while the air filled with the smell of wet earth and algae.

"It’s low," she said. "Today it’s easy."

Jun pushed his glasses up. "My app says the flow is steady. Moderate current."

Nari looked at him. She looked at the water. She looked at his clean shoes.

"Your app," she said, "doesn’t have feet."
pages.image: Jun in white sneakers and a robot T-shirt stands on a sandy riverbank next to Nari in a yellow shirt and green trousers, both looking out at the wide, brown-green river with sandbars rising from the water in the bright morning sun.

pages.text:
Nari pointed at the surface of the water, which looked like a sheet of dark, glossy plastic that had been smoothed flat by a careless hand.

"Brown-green," she said, her voice dropping to a serious, instructional tone. "That means calm. No mud coming down." She moved her finger along the air, tracing a line that matched the current. "See where it slides? Smooth, fast, no ripples? That’s a channel. Deep water."

She pointed to a patch where the surface was broken, the skin of the river wrinkling into small, circular folds.

"Wrinkles," she said. "Stones underneath. Shallows."

Jun nodded, feeling like he was supposed to understand this, though his brain felt like a browser with too many tabs open. He opened his notebook, then closed it again. It felt ridiculous to write down things that were just... water.

"And if I see sticks?" he asked. "Floating sticks?"

Nari’s eyes sharpened. "Rain. Upstream. A lot of rain."

Jun looked at the calm water. It looked like nothing was happening.

"How do you know all this?" he asked. "Where did you learn it?"

Nari shrugged, her shoulders rising and falling in a lazy, unbothered way. She kicked a pebble into the shallows, watching it skip twice before it vanished into the brown-green depth.

"I looked," she said. "For eleven years."
pages.image: Nari points at the rippling river surface while Jun, holding his notebook, watches her gesture with a curious expression, the wide river flowing past them with visible channels and small ripples near the sandy bank.

pages.text:
Tied to a rusty iron ring in the mud sat the boat, small and flat-bottomed, painted a faded color that had once been green but was now just the memory of it.

"The Pear," Nari said.

Jun walked around the hull, noting how the wood was thick and scarred by oars and sun, until he found two orange life vests tucked into the shadow under the seat, looking bright and new like pieces of fruit left too long in the sun.

Harabeoji had mentioned the boat, and he had mentioned the rules. "Vests on," he had said, his voice dry as a twig. "Never alone. And if you are lost, stay with the boat."

Jun felt a spark of delight because in Seoul the rules were apps, full of Terms and Conditions and User Agreements, but here the rule was simple enough to hold in his pocket.

Nari watched his face, seeing the way his eyes lit up as he found order in the chaos, and she frowned because she did not like that he was happy. She liked the river because it was hard, and she liked that it did not make sense to anyone who had not lived beside it.

"You think it’s a game," she said.

"It’s a rule," Jun said. "A good rule."

"Rules," Nari said, "don’t float."
pages.image: The small, faded green wooden boat tied to a rusty ring in the mud, with two bright orange life vests visible under the seat, while Jun and Nari stand nearby on the bank, Jun looking impressed and Nari looking skeptical.

pages.text:
Jun did not argue back. Instead, he pulled his phone from his pouch, where the battery sat at eighty-five percent, and swiped the screen open to show her the sky's view.

"Look," he said.

He held the device up. On the glass, the world appeared from above. The river was a thin, dark line winding through the green valley, while the far field held rows of red peppers drying on mats. The sandbar they stood on looked like a long, pale finger pointing downstream.

Further along that line sat a bridge, and below it, a small, angular shape: a weir.

Nari leaned in close, her nose almost touching the cool glass. She saw the full length of the sandbar, which she had walked past every day for a decade, but had never seen in its entirety. She watched the river curve around the far hill in a way her eyes had missed.

She did not move or speak. For a full minute, she just studied the pixels, the satellite truth of the place she knew by heart.

Jun watched her face change. It was not anger, nor was it boredom. It was a kind of stunned stillness, like a paused game.

"Wow," he said, softly.

Nari’s jaw tightened. She did not say wow. She did not say anything at all.
pages.image: Jun holds his phone up showing a satellite map of the river valley to Nari, who leans in closely to look at the screen, their faces close together in the bright sunlight near the boat.

pages.text:
Nari pulled back, her face settling into that flat, final look she got when a test was over. She looked at the phone, then at the river. The water slid past the stepping stones, brown-green and patient, completely ignoring the glass screen.

"That’s not the river," she said.

"It is," said Jun, pushing his glasses up. "It’s the same river. Just from above."

"The river’s not a picture," Nari said. Her voice was quiet, and it cut through the heat like a cold knife. She turned and walked back toward the corn, her shadow stretching long in the grass.

Jun looked at the river again. The water moved, smooth and deep, carrying the smell of wet earth and old mud. He looked at his phone. The map was still there, clear and correct, showing the world in neat little boxes.

He put the phone away. He did not understand why the river felt so heavy, so real, when the map said it was just a line. He did not tell Nari that he was going to look at that picture again tonight. He did not tell her that he was already trying to memorize the shape of the bend, the place where the water would go if it wanted to run away.

The cicadas screamed. The river slid.
pages.image: Nari walks away toward the tall corn stalks, her back to the viewer, while Jun stands by the boat looking at the river, the wide brown-green water flowing past the sandy bank in the afternoon light.
